title: Selecting CMIP6-Based Future Climate Scenarios for Impact and Adaptation Studies
abstract: Climate change impact assessment studies often use future projections of only a few global climate models (GCMs) due to limited research resources. Here we develop a novel method to select a small subset of GCMs that widely capture the uncertainty range of large ensemble. By applying this method, we select a subset of five GCM projections from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) ensemble for impact and adaptation studies in Japan. At first, we omit GCMs whose global warming projections have been evaluated to be overestimated in the recent literature. Then, we select a subset of five GCMs that widely captures the uncertainty ranges for 8 climate variables and have good performances in present-climate simulations. These selected GCM simulations will be used to provide better climate scenarios for impact and adaptation studies than those in the previous impact assessment project.
problem: Existing methods for selecting a small, representative subset of global climate models for impact studies are inadequate because they fail to simultaneously capture the uncertainty range across multiple variables, consider model performance, and meet project-specific requirements.
method: We propose a method to select a small subset of GCMs by first omitting models with overestimated warming, then choosing a subset that evenly captures the uncertainty range of multiple variables and demonstrates good performance in present-climate simulations, providing a representative basis for impact studies.
task: The task is to develop a novel method to select a small, representative subset of CMIP6 global climate models that captures the wider ensemble's uncertainty range for climate impact and adaptation studies in Japan.
innovation: This paper presents a novel method to select a small, representative subset of CMIP6 climate models by first excluding models with overestimated warming and then selecting those that widely capture the uncertainty range across eight variables and perform well in present-climate simulations.
